content: Epazote, also known as Wormseed, Jesuit's Tea, Mexican Tea, or Herba Sancti Mariæ (scientific name: Chenopodium ambrosioides), is a herbaceous plant native to Central America, South America, and southern Mexico. It can grow up to 2 meters in height and has an irregular branching pattern. Its leaves are oblong-lanceolate in shape and can reach up to 12 cm in length. The plant produces small green flowers that are arranged in a branched panicle at the apex of the stem. In addition to its native regions, epazote is cultivated in warm temperate to subtropical areas of Europe and the United States, including Missouri, New England, and the eastern United States. However, in some cases, it has become an invasive weed. The name epazote is derived from the Nahuatl word epazōtl, which entered the Spanish language. Culinary Uses Epazote is utilized both as a leafy vegetable and as a culinary herb, prized for its strong, pungent flavor. When consumed raw, it has a resinous and medicinal pungency, reminiscent of the licorice-like taste of anise, fennel, or tarragon, but with a much stronger intensity. Its aroma is distinctive and difficult to describe, often compared to a mix of citrus, petroleum, savory, mint, and even putty. Traditionally, epazote is used in Mexican cuisine, particularly with black beans, not only for its flavor but also for its reputed ability to reduce flatulence. Beyond beans, it is used to season a variety of traditional Mexican dishes, including quesadillas and sopes (especially those containing huitlacoche), soups, mole de olla, tamales with cheese and chile, chilaquiles, eggs and potatoes, and enchiladas. Medicinal Uses Epazote has a long history of medicinal use, both as a leafy vegetable and as an herb. It is traditionally believed to prevent flatulence caused by consuming beans. Additionally, it has been used in the treatment of various conditions, including amenorrhea (absence of menstruation), dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation), malaria, chorea (a neurological disorder), hysteria, catarrh (inflammation of mucous membranes), and asthma. The plant is also the source of an essential oil known as oil of chenopodium, which has anthelmintic properties, meaning it is effective in killing intestinal worms. Historically, this oil was listed in the U.S. Pharmacopeia for its use as a deworming agent. Furthermore, epazote has been cited as an antispasmodic and abortifacient. In fact, early research on epazote contributed to the development of the first birth control pills. The essential oil of epazote contains a high concentration of ascaridole (up to 70%), along with other compounds such as limonene, p-cymene, and smaller amounts of monoterpenes and their derivatives, including α-pinene, myrcene, terpinene, thymol, camphor, and trans-isocarveol. Ascaridole, a monoterpene peroxide, is an uncommon constituent in spices and is also found in the plant boldo, which owes much of its character to this compound. Ascaridole is toxic and has a pungent, unpleasant flavor. In its pure form, it is highly explosive and sensitive to shock. Interestingly, the ascaridole content in epazote is reportedly lower in plants grown in Mexico compared to those cultivated in Europe or Asia.
